newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: FEATURE - Jew fish holds promise for Bangladesh.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Jew fish holds promise for Bangladesh.

text.p: Hong Kong's C.W. Lee speaks bitterly about Bangladesh's poor communications system. But he does not mind living in a 30-foot (10-metre) bamboo hut in a coastal village.
Lee has already lived for 12 years in the shabby Bangladeshi village, and says it is for the Jew fish.
"The problem is that I can't contact my office. The telecommunications are awful here," he told Reuters through an interpreter. The language he speaks is a mixture of Chinese, English and Bengali.
Lee is an expert employed by Hong Kong-based Winning Marine Products Ltd, which imports up to 900 tonnes of dried fish from Bangladesh every year.
Two other Hong Kong companies are also importing the dehydrated salted fish from Bangladesh and exporting it to Canada, Taiwan, Japan and China.
"We only buy good quality fish that has demand in other countries," Lee said.
"Many of the Bangladeshi fishermen survive because of our imports. These fish have no demand in the local market."
CURRENT BUSINESS STATUS AND PROSPECTS
Abdul Shukkur, convenor of the Dehydrated Salted Dry Fish Exporters Association, said his union was the sole exporter of dry fish.
The association annually exports around 1,500 tonnes of fish, mostly dried Jew fish, fetching $9 million.
"The people of Chinese origin prefer dried fish. The export of the dried fish has been increasing at a rate of 10-15 percent annually. It has good prospects here," Shukkur said.
"Besides the export earnings, the trade has had tremendous impact on the livings of thousands of people here."
Shukkur said 28,000 fishermen were involved in angling and processing the fish for export.
"The fish are sun-dried. They need chemicals to remove any bad smell and protect the fish from insects. The Hong Kong experts themselves bring in the chemical," he said.
"Importers prefer sun-dried fish. Mechanised drying reduces taste." There are about 12 dry fish processing factories in Bangladesh, he said.
"As for the quality of the fish, we don't have any problems because of the presence of foreign experts," he said.

Shukkur said hundreds of fishermen sailed daily into the Bay of Bengal during low tide and threw about 2,000 hooks with baits to catch the Jew fish, locally called Poa. They weigh about 1.5 kg (3.3 lbs) each.
OLD TRAWLERS AND LACK OF FUNDS
But he said the fishing in the bay was getting difficult because of the poor condition of some 2,000 small trawlers. "We are facing problems with old and mostly unseaworthy trawlers," Shukkur said.
"We need to replace the trawlers with ones fitted with modern machinery and fishing equipment if we want to increase the volume of catch and ensure safety of the fishermen."
Shukkur said he feared business could suffer a setback unless the government offered financial help.
"We need huge funds for modernisation. We have to spend some 20-30 million taka ($47,000-$70,000) a year for the next five years to completely modernise our fleet," he said.
"Nobody recognises our contribution to the economy and there is no praise for our efforts."
